name: Sweet Potato
variety: Species-level edible sweetpotato; no cultivar or ornamental foliage selection assigned
summary: A warm-season vine grown for edible storage roots and, in some contexts, edible leaves. It is botanically unrelated to potato (Solanum tuberosum); cultivars selected for ornamental foliage are not represented.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ipomoea batatas in Convolvulaceae and distinguishes it from true potato, Solanum tuberosum. This species-level entry does not specify a root-flesh color, named cultivar, or ornamental foliage selection.

cultivation.short: Warm-season crop; frost-sensitive and suited to outdoor beds or large containers
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes sweetpotato as frost-sensitive and notes that it can be grown as a groundcover or vine in well-drained soil. Its light and soil recommendations are regional garden guidance, not evidence of a compact hydroponic system fit.

growth.short: Spreading vine with cultivar-dependent foliage and root performance
growth.guidance: NC State Extension reports a spreading, vigorous habit and distinguishes edible-root crop cultivars from ornamental foliage selections. No named cultivar or cultivar-specific mature size is assigned to this species-level record.

harvest.short: Edible storage roots develop in the soil
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension documents edible tuberous roots and notes that production depends on crop selection and growing conditions. A single harvest interval is not supplied here because no cultivar or regional planting schedule is represented.

problems.short: Protect from frost; keep cultivar and food-use identity clear
problems.guidance: NC State Extension identifies frost sensitivity and distinguishes ornamental sweetpotato selections from cultivars grown for edible roots. This profile makes no general disease-resistance claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected extension source describes soil/container and groundcover growing, not a recirculating hydroponic crop system.

evidence.note: Species-level source describes spreading/vining growth; no cultivar-specific habit is assigned.

height.reason: Source dimensions vary by growth form and selection; no single species-level height is selected.

spread.reason: No single mature spread is selected for this cultivar-unspecified identity.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing does not translate to an indoor hydroponic pod layout.

light.reason: The selected source includes regional outdoor light guidance but no canonical indoor grow-light tier or normalized outdoor category is assigned here.

name: Potato
variety: Species-level cultivated potato; no cultivar, market class, or subspecies assigned
summary: A widely grown crop cultivated from seed tubers rather than botanical seed in ordinary home gardens. Thousands of cultivars differ in tuber form and culinary use; none is selected for this species-level entry.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Solanum tuberosum in Solanaceae. Minnesota Extension distinguishes vegetative seed tubers from true botanical seed; the common name seed potato refers to planting stock, not a Seed Profile material.

cultivation.short: Outdoor crop grown in loose, well-drained soil or sufficiently large containers
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes full sun, well-drained soil, and large containers as options; UMN Extension details hilling soil around emerging shoots to cover developing tubers. These are regional soil-crop practices and do not establish home hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Erect foliage produces underground stolons and tubers
growth.guidance: Kew and extension sources describe tuber-bearing underground shoots. Hilling is used in soil production to cover tubers and prevent light exposure; it is not a universal container or hydroponic instruction.

harvest.short: Harvest new or mature tubers according to crop stage
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes early harvest as new potatoes and mature harvest after plants die back. Timing varies with cultivar and region, so the regional calendar is not generalized as a fixed cultivar-free date.

problems.short: Keep developing tubers covered and do not eat green plant parts
problems.guidance: UMN advises hilling to keep shallow tubers from light exposure; NC State warns that green tissues contain solanine and should not be eaten. This safety note is based on the cited sources, not a generalized toxicity claim for unrelated crops.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Selected sources document soil and large-container culture, not a reliable recirculating home hydroponic method.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect stems; this is species-level habit, not cultivar-specific.

height.reason: The selected source provides a range but no cultivar is represented; dimensions are left unresolved rather than implying precision.

spread.reason: No cultivar-specific mature spread is assigned.

spacing.reason: Regional soil row spacing cannot be converted into a hydroponic pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance is not translated into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Garlic
variety: Species-level garlic; hardneck and softneck crop groups not selected; elephant garlic excluded
summary: A bulb crop commonly planted from individual cloves. Hardneck and softneck groups are types within Allium sativum; elephant garlic is a different species and is not included in this identity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Allium sativum in Amaryllidaceae. Utah State Extension distinguishes hardneck and softneck garlic types from elephant garlic, Allium ampeloprasum; neither garlic type is assigned as a named cultivar here.

cultivation.short: Cool-season bulb crop; regional fall planting and well-drained soil guidance
cultivation.guidance: Utah State Extension recommends fall planting in its Utah context and emphasizes fertile, well-drained soil and moisture during growth. Its field spacing and fertilizer rates are not reused as indoor hydroponic instructions.

growth.short: One planted clove produces a bulb; hardneck may form a flowering scape
growth.guidance: Utah State Extension reports one bulb per planted clove and describes differences between hardneck and softneck types. Scape removal is mentioned only as a crop-management option when a scape forms, not as a property of every type.

harvest.short: Harvest when tops yellow, before they become fully dry
harvest.guidance: Utah State Extension recommends lifting bulbs as tops yellow but before they are fully dry, then curing in a shaded warm location. Exact calendar timing depends on planting season and local conditions.

problems.short: Excess moisture near maturity can impair curing and storage
problems.guidance: Utah State Extension warns that excess water as foliage matures can delay curing and cause storage problems, and identifies thrips, onion maggot, and neck rot. These are source-level risks, not claims of resistance or universal susceptibility for a named selection.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source documents soil-grown bulb production, not a recirculating home hydroponic method.

growthHabits.reason: The source describes bulb and leaf growth but does not map this identity to the controlled growth-habit vocabulary.

height.reason: No cultivar-specific mature dimensions are selected.

spread.reason: No cultivar-specific mature spread is selected.

spacing.reason: Field row and clove spacing are not hydroponic pod-spacing guidance.

name: Ginger
summary: A tropical rhizomatous perennial grown for its aromatic edible rhizome. In cooler climates it can be container-grown or treated seasonally; selected sources do not establish a recirculating hydroponic method.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Zingiber officinale in Zingiberaceae and identifies the rhizome as the spice source. No named cultivar or commercial ginger type is selected.

cultivation.short: Tropical plant; container culture is possible with warm, protected conditions
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes container growing and advises bringing plants indoors before temperatures fall below 50°F in its regional context. It warns that cold, wet conditions can cause root rot; do not infer a particular hydroponic system from container tolerance.

growth.short: Clumping, spreading foliage emerges from underground rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes an upright, clumping and spreading plant and gives species-level dimensions. The profile retains a cultivar-unspecified scope and does not imply a compact indoor selection.

harvest.short: Harvest selected rhizomes while allowing the clump to continue growing
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension says several rhizomes may be harvested while leaving the rest of the clump growing. Young and mature rhizomes differ in texture; no fixed home harvest date is assigned.

problems.short: Avoid cold, wet growing media that can promote root rot
problems.guidance: NC State Extension identifies root rot risk in cold and/or wet conditions. It also notes that strong full sun may cause brown leaf tips and poor growth in its guidance; no disease-resistance trait is asserted.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Container culture is documented, but no selected source establishes performance in a recirculating home hydroponic system.

evidence.note: NC State Extension describes clumping and spreading habit at species scope.

name: Turmeric
summary: A tropical rhizomatous perennial cultivated for its aromatic yellow-orange rhizome. NC State Extension reports that it is propagated by rhizome division and that its flowers are sterile; no Seed Profile is appropriate for this crop identity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Curcuma longa in Zingiberaceae and lists Curcuma domestica as a synonym. NC State Extension describes the culinary rhizome and does not assign a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Warm, humid growing conditions; container culture can require substantial space
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes warm, humid conditions, moist but well-drained soil and container growing. Rhizomes can enlarge enough to split a container; these observations do not establish indoor hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Upright clump with broad leaves from branched rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State Extension reports an upright perennial herb with broad leaves and mature height and width ranges. These are species-level regional dimensions, not cultivar-specific guarantees.

harvest.short: Harvest rhizomes as foliage wilts and dries
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes harvesting rhizomes in fall as foliage begins to wilt and dry. This seasonal timing reflects its regional growing guidance and is not generalized to every climate.

problems.short: Avoid cold and poor drainage; cut rhizomes may stain skin and fabric
problems.guidance: The selected Extension source describes turmeric as a warm-climate plant and notes yellow dye staining and possible allergic skin reaction. It reports no serious insect or disease problems in its regional account; that is not a universal resistance claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Container and soil culture are documented; no recirculating hydroponic performance evidence was selected.
